item.title: Solar System Surface Technosignatures: Searching for Signs of Artificial Design on Extraterrestrial Terrain
item.description: arXiv:2610.28687v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial radio emissions have historically been a major focus of technosignature searches. Here, we apply an anthropological lens to expand this scope to surface technosignatures: non-random, intentional patterning on planetary terrain, similar to long-lasting human-made landscapes and monuments on Earth. On geologically inactive bodies such as the Moon and Mars, artificial traces and patterns could potentially remain visible for hundreds of millions of years. We discuss two recent developments that make this search timely: high-resolution imaging datasets, such as those produced by the HiRISE camera on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), and ML-based anomaly-detection methods. Finally, we list two possible approaches to developing a model capable of searching for these surface technosignatures: a supervised and an unsupervised one. Complemented by LiDAR, ground-penetrating radar, and reflectance spectroscopy, these methods would enable the first quantitative upper limits on surface technosignatures while yielding ancillary benefits for planetary science.
item.dc:creator: Ana Henrique, Sofia Sheikh, Benjamin Fields

item.title: Data-driven characterisation of variable source light curves with multimodal representation learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.29412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surveys such as the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) produce light curves for hundreds of millions of variables. Their characterisation traditionally relies on supervised classifiers with hand-crafted features and curated labels, limiting them to predefined taxonomies and individual surveys. We present a general, survey-agnostic framework that characterises variable sources without labelled training data, producing low-dimensional representations of light curve properties such as amplitude, periodicity, and asymmetry. A multimodal architecture combines two complementary views, a Transformer encoder on raw observations and a convolutional neural network on a generalised Lomb-Scargle periodogram. Each light curve is randomly split into two temporal halves as independent views, and the branches are trained jointly with VICReg to produce embeddings invariant across halves while keeping each dimension informative. We evaluate on 37 006 ZTF sources spanning 14 variable star classes in four broad physical categories. A linear classifier on the frozen 64-dimensional embeddings achieves 77.1% balanced accuracy for classes and 90.5% for broad categories. Combining both branches improves balanced accuracy by up to 14.9 percentage points over the best single modality, confirming their complementarity. Interpretable light curve properties are encoded on distinct dimensions, and within-class analysis reveals physical substructure unresolved by reference labels. Retraining on ZTF g and i bands without modification reproduces the main results, and concatenating multi-band embeddings improves balanced accuracy to 86.1%. The framework needs no labels, phase folding, or survey-specific preprocessing and applies directly to other surveys with different cadences and wavelength coverage.
item.dc:creator: M. Madar\'asz, G. Marton, M. Audard

item.title: Optimization of Petal-Shaped Occulters for Exo-Earth Observation
item.description: arXiv:2610.29628v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Petal-shaped occulters are giant, formation-flying optical devices designed for use in space astronomy. Their primary function is to block the intense starlight to enable the direct observation of exoplanets, a process challenged by the extreme contrast ratio (lower than 1e-10 for an exo-Earth). This study focuses on optimizing the shape of the occulter in order to significantly reduce Fresnel diffraction. For a circular occulter, the diffraction pattern shows the bright Arago spot. Nevertheless, we construct an apodized occulter as the weighted sum of circular occulters of various diameters, owing to the fact that their diffraction are complex amplitudes which can, with adequate weighting, interfere with each other in such a way as to form a resulting diffraction pattern with a very dark central area. This basis of circular occulters allows the use of a simple analytical form for their Fresnel diffraction. First, occulter diameters are fixed on a regularly sampled linear scale, and the weights are obtained by minimizing a quadratic criterion. An improvement is then obtained using a combined optimization over the weights and the diameters sizes. Eventually, the apodized profile is used to design the petal-shaped occulter for physical imple- mentation constraints. The resulting rejection rates are comparable to the results obtained using SISTER ( http://sister.caltech.edu ), which uses a completely different non-parametric approach.
item.dc:creator: Simon Prunet, C\'eline Theys, Claude Aime

item.title: In search of the third dimension in Compton X-ray polarimeters
item.description: arXiv:2610.29900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Compton polarimeters are typically designed to be sensitive only to the azimuthal angle of the scattered photon, ignoring the scattering angle. Such a 2-dimensional reconstruction of the event is pursued for both simplicity and because the polarization of the incident photon influences only the azimuthal response of the instrument. While this is true for on-axis sources, when the source starts to be off-axis of several degrees the azimuthal response of the instrument is effectively a convolution of the azimuthal and polar scattering angles: measuring the latter would provide a better sensitivity and smaller systematic effects. In this contribution, we will present a design which allows to estimate the scattering angle in a Compton polarimeter through the read-out of the light signal at the two ends of scintillator bars. Such a design is being tested with a representative set-up and first results on the performance are presented.

item.title: In-orbit anomaly and recovery of IXPE detector 2
item.description: arXiv:2610.29920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer (IXPE) is a joint NASA-ASI mission launched in December 2021 to measure the linear polarization of celestial X-ray sources in the 2-8 keV energy range. The payload comprises three identical telescopes, each combining grazing-incidence X-ray optics with a focal-plane photoelectric polarimeter based on the Gas Pixel Detector technology. On 14 April 2025, the second detector experienced an anomaly that significantly altered the electrical behavior of the ASIC responsible for reading out the photoelectron track images. In this contribution, we describe the effect of the anomaly on the instrumental response and the actions taken to mitigate its effects and recover the scientific observations of the instrument.

item.title: Cosmic Ray Observations using Coincident Scintillator and Radio Signals with the Beamforming Elevated Array for COsmic Neutrinos (BEACON)
item.description: arXiv:2610.29923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: At energies above 100 PeV, coherent radio frequency (RF) emission across the 10 -- 1000 MHz band from cosmic particle-induced atmospheric showers becomes increasingly dominant, making radio detection a powerful probe at ultrahigh energies. The Beamforming Elevated Array for COsmic Neutrinos (BEACON) considers mountaintop phased radio arrays to monitor large areas at the horizon for upward-going geomagnetic emission in the 30 -- 80 MHz band produced as a consequence of Earth-skimming tau neutrinos. As part of ongoing efforts to measure the sensitivity of BEACON to such signals, the BEACON prototype identifies cosmic rays through the same emission mechanism. Prior to 2023, BEACON operated a four-antenna prototype, which successfully demonstrated identification of coherent and impulsive sources using a beamforming RF trigger. In 2023, we upgraded the instrument to six newly designed antennas and added an independent scintillator array to cross-validate radio-detectable cosmic rays. This work details the observation of 22 candidate cosmic-ray events in a scintillator-coincidence-triggered dataset using selection cuts based on expected radio characteristics. A simulation of the hybrid-instrument performance verifies this observation rate to within an order of magnitude. We estimate a background of 0.11 events by applying the selection cuts to synthetic datasets of uncorrelated radio-scintillator pairs that are randomly formed using fixed-rate software-triggered data. The reconstructed signal polarization angles are consistent with pure geomagnetic emission compared to various background classes.

item.title: A design concept for the High Resolution Imager on the Habitable Worlds Observatory
item.description: arXiv:2610.29957v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) will be NASA's next flagship astrophysics mission, designed to search for signs of life on planets around nearby stars and conduct transformational science across astrophysics. Its High Resolution Imager (HRI) is not only the observatory's main imaging camera, but also provides grism spectroscopy and sub-microarcsecond astrometry, as well as the observatory's fine guidance, wavefront sensing and pupil imaging. We present a design concept for HRI, developed during concurrent design sessions by flowing down science requirements within the envelope of NASA's EAC-1 telescope architecture. Light from a 3'x2' field is collimated by two mirrors, then divided by a dichroic for simultaneous observations in an ultraviolet-to-visible arm covering 200-900 nm and a near-infrared arm covering 0.9-2.2 um. By minimising the number of reflective surfaces upstream of the dichroic, our optical design maximises throughput and stability, while reducing wavefront error. Readout modes can be chosen in orbit to image the entire field in exposures of at least 10 seconds, or in smaller windows for observations up to 1 kHz. Throughout, we emphasise the interplay between subsystems that couple design choices.

item.title: The Pandora SmallSat: Target Selection and Early Science
item.description: arXiv:2610.30028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Pandora spacecraft is a smallsat selected in NASA's inaugural class of Pioneers missions. The aim of the Pandora mission is to disentangle stellar activity signals from exoplanet atmospheric transmission spectroscopy measurements. Pandora accomplishes this goal with its combined visible photometry and NIR spectroscopy that observe each target in the prime mission for 10 separate transit observations, each spanning 24 hours at a time. Targets were carefully selected for the Pandora prime mission. Pandora is specifically studying planets around low-mass stellar hosts (K and M dwarf stars) spanning a range of rotation periods and activity levels. The planets range in size from 1.5 - 15 Earth radii and orbital periods ranging from 1.7 - 11.5 days. In addition to the 10 transit visits planned for each of the 20 prime mission targets, Pandora is observing a number of auxiliary targets encompassing a variety of science topics. This includes topics such as stellar activity and young systems, transit timing variations of exoplanets, brown dwarf compositions, exoplanet phase curves, etc. We will discuss the selection of these targets, how they have been scheduled to fill in gaps in prime mission operations, and early science results. If the mission is extended, there is further opportunity for accomplishing additional science. Here we will discuss the possible options for extended mission operations and science.

item.title: Noisy Pipelines I: An end-to-end pipeline to perform multivariate noise inference for LISA
item.description: arXiv:2610.28726v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Instrumental data from the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) must be post-processed prior to any global-fit based analysis. For example, it is critical to filter, downsample, segment and window the data in order to perform inference of both the signal and noise parameters in the frequency domain. Each step alters the noise process, requiring a correction to the noise covariance matrix that describes the underlying data stream. We present $\texttt{lisa-noise}$, a JAX-based noise inference pipeline that returns a spectral estimate of the noise process subject to post-processing effects. We fit splines to the underlying secondary noises and fit the full multivariate $3 \times 3$ covariance matrix of the Michelson channels. We assume unequal and non-constant arm-lengths throughout. The drift of the zeros of the transfer functions, a non-stationary effect, is captured by averaging the transfer functions over a number of epochs within each segment. On 30 days of conditioned simulated data, a likelihood evaluation costs $3\,$ms on a current laptop for a 7 day segment. A gradient-based fit from a tight prior recovers the injected spectra in a fraction of a second. A multi-start search over large priors $\pm 10$ in $\log_{10}$ centred on the simulated truth obtains a noise estimate consistent with the data, verified by Bayesian techniques. The fitted covariance whitens the conditioned data in every band and through every zero of the transfer functions, in a form that global-fit pipelines can use directly.
item.dc:creator: Ollie Burke, Joseph Bayley, Charlie Hoy, Laura Nuttall

item.title: Arepo-CD: Coupling Collisional $N$-Body Dynamics with Moving-Mesh Magnetohydrodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.28727v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Star formation is a hierarchical, clustered process in turbulent giant molecular clouds (GMCs), where close stellar encounters can strongly affect cluster evolution and feedback. However, gravitational softening in many hydrodynamic simulations of GMCs limits the treatment of these encounters. We present Arepo-CD (Collisional Dynamics), a framework that couples star-by-star collisional $N$-body dynamics to the moving-mesh magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) code Arepo. Star-star interactions use unsoftened gravity, while interactions involving gas or collisionless components remain softened. Compact stellar subsystems are identified on the fly and evolved with a fourth-order forward symplectic integrator and slow-down algorithmic regularization coupled to the native Arepo timestep hierarchy. Benchmark tests against the collisional $N$-body code PeTar show good agreement in cluster core collapse and subsequent expansion, radial density profiles, and stellar velocity distributions. Coupled to the Rigel star formation and feedback model, Arepo-CD follows cluster formation and early evolution in radiation MHD simulations of a $10^5~M_\odot$ turbulent molecular cloud. In the fiducial GMC comparison, the collisional and softened-gravity runs yield similar star formation histories and integrated star formation efficiencies. Nevertheless, close gravitational encounters during the embedded phase generate a substantial runaway population, with a velocity tail extending beyond 100 km/s. Ejected massive stars redistribute radiative feedback into the surrounding lower-density medium and produce a more extended distribution of heated gas. Arepo-CD provides a practical and computationally efficient framework for studying collisional stellar dynamics and its coupling to gas evolution and feedback during star cluster formation in realistic galactic environments.
item.dc:creator: Chuizheng Kong, Hui Li, Long Wang, Yunwei Deng, Elizabeth Moreno-Hilario

item.title: Prior volume effect inflates the gravitational-wave background in pulsar timing arrays
item.description: arXiv:2610.28739v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) have found evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background (GWB) whose amplitude exceeds most predictions based on supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs). Using NANOGrav 15-year data, we show that a substantial part of this excess arises from a prior volume effect. The GWB amplitude is constrained mainly by the pulsars' auto-correlations, where the GWB is degenerate with each pulsar's intrinsic red noise. By decomposing the GWB posterior, we find that marginalizing over the standard log-uniform red-noise priors introduces a prior volume term that favors a stronger GWB, pulling the inferred amplitude more than $2\sigma$ above the maximum-likelihood estimate. The Hellings-Downs (HD) cross-correlations, which measure the GWB alone, are not strong enough to counter the volume term. The profile likelihood, a cross-correlation-only estimator, and priors that are uniform in power or informed by the pulsar population all avoid or reduce this effect and lower the amplitude into agreement with SMBHBs. The revised priors also yield a steeper GWB spectrum closer to the SMBHB predictions, strengthen the evidence for HD correlations, and weaken the preference for new-physics sources over SMBHBs.
item.dc:creator: Biwei Dai, Matias Zaldarriaga, Yacine Ali-Ha\"{\i}moud

item.title: Systematic Uncertainties in Rocky Exoplanet Reflected Light from Incomplete Laboratory BRDF Measurements
item.description: arXiv:2610.28755v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The first observations of short-period rocky exoplanets have initiated the era of terrestrial exoplanet characterization. The interpretation of these observations relies on forward models used in atmospheric and surface retrieval frameworks. While atmospheric modeling is supported by extensive laboratory datasets of molecular opacities, the experimental basis for rocky surface characterization remains limited. Most reflectance libraries of planetary analog materials provide spectra measured at a single illumination and viewing geometry, constraining the spectral behavior but not its full angular scattering properties. We show that incomplete angular coverage in laboratory bidirectional reflectance measurements introduces an intrinsic systematic uncertainty in the interpretation of rocky exoplanet observations. We demonstrate that multiple combinations of photometric parameters can reproduce the same laboratory reflectance spectrum while predicting different angular scattering behaviors and disk-integrated observables. We propagate this non-uniqueness to reflected-light phase curves, geometric albedos, and planet-star contrast ratios between $0.5$--$1.7\,\mu$m, representative of the spectral range targeted by future direct-imaging missions such as the HWO. We find that single-geometry laboratory spectra produce large uncertainties in predicted signals, particularly at small phase angles. Simplified assumptions adopted in exoplanet studies, such as isotropic scattering can additionally introduce systematic biases. Using multi-angular laboratory measurements from the Bloomsburg University Goniometer dataset, we show that the uncertainty in predicted observables collapses once angular scattering behavior is directly constrained. Our results demonstrate that multi-angular measurements are required to construct physically predictive reflected-light models of rocky exoplanets.
item.dc:creator: Leonardos Gkouvelis, Michael K. Shepard, Paul Helfenstein, Francisco J. Pozuelos, Renyu Hu

item.title: PIANISTpy: A JAX-based Python package for velocity-anisotropic astrophysical equilibrium models
item.description: arXiv:2610.28758v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The hierarchical assembly of dark matter haloes and galaxies via mergers and anisotropic mass accretion naturally imprints non-trivial velocity anisotropy onto haloes and galaxies, an empirical fact emerging from cosmological simulations. However, dynamical studies based on idealised numerical simulations typically assume isotropic velocity distributions for the systems studied. This is mainly because no tools exist to construct anisotropic initial conditions with fully self-consistent (i.e., physical and instability-free) truncation boundary conditions for finite spatial extents. Here we present the first such analytical framework that performs truncation in phase space, with two distinct approaches to guarantee either the monotonicity of output distribution functions or identical truncated density profiles. We additionally present the open-source JAX-based GPU-accelerated Python package PIANISTpy (Particle Initial conditions with ANISoTropy) for constructing spherical, non-rotating initial conditions, supporting arbitrary double-power-law analytical radial density profiles and a library of analytical anisotropy profiles. This framework further permits the construction of systems with non-analytical anisotropy profiles via an arbitrary linear superposition of all implemented analytical anisotropy models as basis functions. PIANISTpy also outputs 3D velocity profiles and line-of-sight-integrated observables with end-to-end differentiability for rapid gradient-based Monte Carlo inference, and self-consistent local dark matter velocity distributions of anisotropic haloes beyond the unphysical Maxwell-Boltzmann simplification adopted in terrestrial detection experiments. We discuss use cases and demonstrate PIANISTpy's orders-of-magnitude higher numerical solver accuracy and superior dynamical stability of particle initial conditions relative to existing tools, including galpy and AGAMA.
item.dc:creator: Barry T. Chiang, Frank C. van den Bosch, Hsi-Yu Schive

item.title: KROME-X: a GPU-ready library for chemistry and microphysics in astrophysical simulations
item.description: arXiv:2610.28917v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: KROME is a Python pre-processor that writes a complete Fortran solver of chemistry and microphysics for each chemical network, widely used in astrophysical simulations. We introduce here KROME-X, a complete rewrite of KROME in modern C++, which incorporates updated physics. A code generator translates a declarative network description into a compact core (rates, right-hand side, analytic Jacobian, thermal terms, and tables), which a fixed, header-only runtime integrates with a C++ port of the `backward differentiation formula' method of CVODE (SUNDIALS). The physics is validated against legacy KROME and independent references. On the legacy test cases KROME-X reproduces legacy KROME to the accuracy of the solvers, wherever the physics is the same, and is up to 13.5 times faster at equal tolerance. On NVIDIA A100 GPUs, it can outperform its share of a computing node from a few thousand cells per call, with the highest throughput (5 to 30) obtained for $10^5$ cells per batch. Networks of hundreds of species still run faster on the CPU due to the GPU's limited memory capacity. The new version also includes, among other changes, on-the-fly co-evolution of a photon field alongside chemistry, which conserves photons exactly; the secondary ionizations using the photoelectron energy of each absorption; dust evolution in size and temperature with a true grain energy equation; line cooling rates rebuilt from current atomic and molecular data, and incorporating optical thickness effects. KROME-X therefore represents the natural successor of KROME and provides a portable, extensible framework for astrochemical kinetics on both CPUs and GPUs for future hydrodynamic simulations.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Lupi, Tommaso Grassi, Stefano Bovino

item.title: Dual-Phase Flow Matching for Probabilistic Source Detection and Measurement in Astronomical Images
item.description: arXiv:2610.28919v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Using the largest digital camera ever built, the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory's 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will image over half the night sky. Most astronomical analyses of LSST data operate not on images but on catalogs derived from them: tables of light sources detailing their positions, fluxes (colors and brightnesses), and types (e.g., star, galaxy). At LSST's imaging depths, light sources often overlap visually, so the configuration of sources in each image is itself uncertain. Nevertheless, LSST's cataloging pipeline commits to a single source configuration, which can bias downstream analyses. Here, we instead approximate a posterior distribution over source configurations. Our posterior approximation is a continuous-time Markov process (CTMP) fitted by generator matching, an extension of flow matching to non-Euclidean state spaces. This CTMP generates a source configuration in two phases: it detects light sources in the first and measures them in the second. On simulated LSST-like data, the proposed method produces better posterior approximations than five comparison methods: two Markov chain Monte Carlo methods that run thousands of times more slowly at survey scales; two neural posterior estimation methods; and one ablation of the proposed method that lacks the dual-phase structure. Applied to LSST Data Preview 1 (DP1), the first public release of Rubin imaging, the proposed method alone recovers small-scale galaxy clustering in agreement with higher-resolution Hubble imaging and reports uncertainty that remains calibrated against that reference as blending increases. We deliver a probabilistic catalog of the Extended Chandra Deep Field South region, one of the most extensively studied extragalactic fields, and use it to characterize the galaxy color-magnitude distribution.
item.dc:creator: Yicun Duan, Jeffrey Regier

item.title: How general relativity stacks up: Testing gravity by coherently combining gravitational-wave observations
item.description: arXiv:2610.29247v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A core mission of gravitational-wave astronomy is to test general relativity (GR) in the high-curvature, high-velocity regime. The field has already seen significant progress in this space, though a remaining challenge is how to combine data from a population of binary mergers. This can both boost the significance of potential GR violations, and develop a phenomenological picture of how deviations manifest in different mergers. We propose a framework to coherently combine gravitational-wave measurements to build a population-level test of physics beyond GR. We assume that deviations from GR are (i) strongest near the merger, (ii) vary smoothly with the total mass of the binary, and (iii) are most prominent in the $\ell=|m|=2$ mode. While these assumptions do not describe every possible deviation of GR, they provide us with a plausible starting point upon which a more general framework can be built. We apply our framework to 28 high signal-to-noise ratio binary black hole mergers from LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA's Fifth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog, finding no evidence for deviations from GR. Our framework allows one to show how deviations could vary as a function of total mass of the system. We argue that such a reconstruction can be used to convincingly distinguish between systematic waveform errors and genuine GR violations.
item.dc:creator: Lachlan Passenger, Nir Guttman, Paul D. Lasky, Eric Thrane

item.title: B-fields In STar-forming Region Observations (BISTRO): Technical Foundations for Quantitative 450/850 $\mu$m JCMT SCUBA-2/POL-2 Polarimetry
item.description: arXiv:2610.29273v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present five technical validations of SCUBA-2/POL-2 polarimetry on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope at 450 and 850 $\mu$m, using 174 archival fields in 69 molecular cloud regions and subsets appropriate to each test. Extended-source calibration avoids a deterministic shift of $\Delta\beta=-1.05$ in the dust emissivity index $\beta$ that would result from calibrating extended emission using peak brightness. We modeled Stokes $I$ noise with additive and signal-dependent components. The measured median ratio of surface-brightness noise at 450/850 $\mu$m is 25. Independent tests of Stokes $Q,U$ noise support approximately equal additive variances and weak error correlations, providing a basis for propagating polarization uncertainties. Corrections determined for individual fields reduce additive zero-level offsets of order $1$ mJy arcsec$^{-2}$ in the 450 $\mu$m Stokes $Q$ and $U$ intensities. The three-step regression leaves a median combined residual amplitude of $0.07$ mJy arcsec$^{-2}$. Independent comparisons with SOFIA/HAWC+ at 154 and 214 $\mu$m support the correction in strongly affected fields. We matched the 450 $\mu$m maps to the modeled 850 $\mu$m beam and the common $12.6''$-$300''$ range of angular scales. We compared three reductions of the same 450 $\mu$m observations across 30 sources. Taking the median angular residual relative to the final product for each source, we find that beam matching reduces the median over sources from $6.3^\circ$ to $4.7^\circ$. After matching, 29 of the 30 sources have median residuals below $10^\circ$. We also quantified how residual $Q/U$ offsets propagate in ratios of polarization fractions, differences in spectral indices, and polarization angles. These validations provide procedures and quantitative references for interpreting POL-2 measurements and combining them with polarimetry at other wavelengths.

item.title: B-fields In STar-forming Region Observations (BISTRO): Dual-Wavelength Constraints on Size-Dependent Grain Alignment in Star-Forming Regions
item.description: arXiv:2610.29285v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We compared 450 and 850 $\mu$m POL-2 observations from the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope at $12.6''$ resolution. The median absolute difference in polarization angle between bands is $6.7^\circ$ across 21 regions. For total intensity $I\propto\nu^\alpha$ and polarized intensity $PI\propto\nu^\gamma$, 24-27 of 35 regions have $\gamma<\alpha$, allowing for $3\sigma$ limits on weak polarized intensities. The median $\gamma-\alpha$ is $-0.51$, ranging from $-0.57$ to $-0.45$ under these limits. The ratio of polarization fractions is $P_{450}/P_{850}=0.69\pm0.02_{\rm sys}\pm0.03_{\rm stat}$, with no detected dependence on the angle difference. We suggest that the dependence of alignment on grain size offers the simplest explanation of these findings. For optically thin components sharing a polarization angle and opacity law, temperature mixing reproduces the median $-0.51$ only if the warm dust is polarized less efficiently than the cold dust. If the cold dust is at 10 K or warmer and the warm dust at 40 K or cooler, the median requires a ratio of warm to cold effective polarization efficiencies $r\lesssim0.18$. We tested mixtures with opacity index $\beta=2$ in four fields against Herschel dust temperatures and Green Bank Ammonia Survey kinetic temperatures. We assumed equal gas and dust temperatures, ammonia tracing cold gas, and model ranges of 3-20 K for cold dust and 25-40 K for warm dust carrying at most half the mass. Mixtures matching both temperatures cannot reproduce $\gamma-\alpha$ within $1\sigma$ in three fields, including OMC 2 tentatively, even for $r=0$. Allowing warm dust at 10-100 K and up to 95% of the mass permits solutions only for $r\leq0.041$. To explain these three fields by temperature mixing, we need wider model ranges and a very strong contrast in polarization efficiency. The origin of this contrast remains undetermined.

item.title: simesh: A Python Framework for Quantitative Analysis of Native AMR Data from MPI-AMRVAC
item.description: arXiv:2610.29333v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) is widely used in large-scale astrophysical simulations, but the resulting multilevel data are challenging to analyze quantitatively. We present simesh, an independent Python framework for quantitative analysis of cell-centered fields on block-structured AMR meshes. The current implementation targets three-dimensional Cartesian datasets from MPI-AMRVAC and compatible AGILE snapshots, preserving the native AMR hierarchy and connecting complementary scientific diagnostics within a common numerical representation. The framework combines Python workflow interfaces with compiled Cython kernels, supporting efficient analysis on AMR meshes. We compare native AMR analysis with a VTK point-data conversion and uniform-grid resampling, which shows that changes in data association, interpolation support, and differentiation scale affect both sampled magnetic fields and derived current densities. Small differences in the sampled primary field can become more pronounced in derivative-based quantities, particularly near coarse-fine interfaces. The applications combine field diagnostics, tracing, regional statistics, and line-of-sight integration on the same native AMR representation. simesh makes these operations available through reusable Python interfaces for reproducible analysis of multiscale simulation data.
item.dc:creator: Hao Wu, Jinhan Guo, Rony Keppens, Yang Guo

item.title: Orientation-dependent sensitivity of the all-sky all-frequency gravitational-wave radiometer search to continuous-wave sources
item.description: arXiv:2610.29384v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The all-sky all-frequency (ASAF) gravitational-wave radiometer search cross-correlates the data of two detectors with equal weight on the $+$ and $\times$ tensor polarizations. This is optimal for an unpolarized stochastic background, but not for continuous-wave (CW) sources, whose polarization depends on the inclination angle $\iota$ and the polarization angle $\psi$. Unless the source is seen face-on, the search measures less power than a face-on source with the same intrinsic amplitude, and underestimates its strength. The ratio of the two powers, the projection factor $\mu^2(\iota,\psi)$, is known from earlier radiometer studies. We show how $\mu^2$ enters the ASAF statistic, derive its exact dependence on $\psi$, and prove that its average over orientations is exactly $2/5$, independent of sky position, baseline geometry, noise weighting, and frequency. We apply the formalism to four simulated pulsar signals at four sky positions, with polarization from circular to nearly linear, injected into the LIGO detectors during the second observing run (O2). A nearly edge-on injection is measured with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of $5.20$, below the threshold of $6.19$, while the same signal seen face-on would have an SNR of $31.1 \pm 6.0$. Bayesian upper limits on the strain amplitude $h_0$, marginalized over orientation and calibration uncertainty, are $2.7$ to $2.9$ times the face-on values. For the $505$ sub-threshold candidates of the first part of the fourth LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA observing run (O4a), the upper limits increase by a factor of $2.5$ to $2.9$, and a source of the same strength would reach threshold only when inclined by less than $34.7^{\circ}$ to $50.3^{\circ}$ from face-on. The measured SNR and the significance of every candidate are unchanged.
item.dc:creator: Stavros Venikoudis, Giacomo Bruno

item.title: Probabilistic Machine Learning for Short-Term Atmospheric Seeing Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2610.29654v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate short-term forecasting of atmospheric seeing is of significant interest for astronomical observations and free-space optical communication systems, where rapid variations in optical turbulence can affect system performance and operational planning. In this work, we benchmark machine learning models for predicting atmospheric seeing up to two hours in advance, with a particular focus on probabilistic forecasting and uncertainty quantification. We compare two probabilistic approaches, Gaussian Processes (GPs) and a normalizing-flow- based model (FloTS), against deterministic recurrent neural network (RNN) and long short-term memory (LSTM) baselines. All models are trained and evaluated on seeing measurements from the Maunakea summit. We assess the models using both deterministic metrics, including the root mean square error and the Pearson correlation coefficient, and probabilistic metrics that evaluate the quality and calibration of predictive uncertainty estimates. The results show that deep learning approaches outperform standard recurrent networks for short-term forecasting, with LSTM and FloTS achieving the best overall predictive accuracy. While Gaussian Processes provide a useful probabilistic baseline, their predictive distributions are limited by the Gaussian assumption. FloTS combines competitive forecasting accuracy with flexible uncertainty quantification and produces the most informative probabilistic forecasts.
item.dc:creator: Mary-Joe Medlej, Rahul Srinivasan, Simon Prunet, Aziz Ziad, Christophe Giordano

item.title: SpinOctopus: A Versatile, User-Friendly, and Extensible Public Code for General-Relativistic Ray-Tracing in axisymmetric spacetime
item.description: arXiv:2610.29800v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Relativistic ray-tracing algorithms serve as indispensable numerical tools for investigating gravitational theories and high-energy astrophysics. In this paper, we develop and release SpinOctopus, a versatile relativistic ray-tracing code tailored for arbitrary axisymmetric spacetimes, powered by a Fortran/Python hybrid architecture and OpenMP multi-threading acceleration. This numerical toolkit is capable of simulating timelike orbits and their corresponding light curves, null geodesics, as well as black hole images illuminated by a wide array of phenomenological sources, including geometrically thin and thick accretion disks, geometrically thin tilted disks, relativistic jets, spherically symmetric accretion flows, and point sources. To execute these tasks, users are solely required to specify the covariant metric tensor of the target spacetime and the simulation parameters within a dedicated configuration file. Benefiting from our customized adaptive step-size strategy for geodesic integration, SpinOctopus achieves an impressive processing efficiency of $\sim 800$ rays per second per thread on an Intel Core i7-14700 platform when simulating geometrically thick accretion disk images. Furthermore, the code provides transparent interfaces, allowing users to seamlessly modify the geometric and kinematic properties of the light sources. Additional capabilities, such as simulating Fe K${\alpha}$ fluorescent line profiles and geometrically thick tilted accretion disk images, will be introduced in future releases of the framework.
item.dc:creator: Shiyang Hu, Dan Li, Chen Deng, Lina Zhang, Wenfu Cao

item.title: A Broadband Room-Temperature Design for the Einstein Telescope
item.description: arXiv:2610.29863v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The unique underground location of the Einstein Telescope (ET) is expected to substantially suppress seismic and gravity-gradient noise, providing a favorable environment for gravitational-wave detection at low frequencies compared with surface-based observatories. The baseline ET design aims to achieve broadband sensitivity through a xylophone configuration, in which separate cryogenic and room-temperature interferometers are optimised for low- and high-frequency gravitational-wave detection. However, achieving the target low-frequency sensitivity introduces substantial technical complexity caused by vertical suspension thermal noise, vibrations of the cryocooler, and detuned optical configuration. In this paper, we demonstrate an alternative, entirely room-temperature, fully resonant, single-interferometer architecture that addresses these challenges and achieves broadband sensitivity superior to that of the conventional ET xylophone configuration. Using mature fused-silica suspension technology, recent advances in optical coatings, and novel inertial isolation, we show that 4-m-long fused-silica fibres can meet the required suspension thermal-noise performance. We further demonstrate that vibrations, optical rigidity, and quantum back-action noise can be controlled through appropriate design of the interferometer, test mass suspensions, optical seismometers, and quantum states.
item.dc:creator: Teng Zhang, Amit Singh Ubhi, Huan Yang, Alan V. Cumming, Mark Barton, Angus Bell, Fabio Bergamin, Giacomo Bruno, Katherine L. Dooley, Johannes Eichholz, Mariana Fazio, Aaron Goodwin-Jones, James Hough, Keiko Kokeyama, Haixing Miao, Xingrui Peng, Geraint Pratten, Stuart Reid, Sheila Rowan, Patricia Schmidt, Alberto Vecchio, Giles Hammond, Hartmut Grote, Denis Martynov

item.title: Validation of Satellite Lifetime Predictions at Leonid Space
item.description: arXiv:2601.02453v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper validates Leonid Space's satellite lifetime prediction pipeline through a backtesting campaign of 1283 deorbited satellites spanning six decades of spaceflight, showing that it accurately recreates their last year of flight. The pipeline combines a custom high-speed orbit propagator, ballistic coefficient estimation from on-orbit TLE data, atmospheric density corrections from data assimilation, custom space weather forecasts, and probabilistic Monte Carlo analysis. Validation proceeds in four steps that progressively remove the benefit of hindsight: starting from a "perfect knowledge" scenario using actual space weather data and ephemerides, we gradually replace historical data with contemporary predictions to arrive at a fully predictive scenario analogous to a deorbit prediction performed for a spacecraft flying today. These forecasts are scored using the continuously ranked probability score and root mean square calibration error, yielding a median one-year prediction accuracy of 2.4 days (0.7%) with perfect knowledge and 35.3 days (9.7%) in the fully predictive scenario. Solar flux forecasts contribute 75% of the variance in our predictions, dominating all other sources of error. To our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive backtesting of long-term satellite lifetime predictions that reports quantitative results for the fully predictive case, and it establishes a new framework for scoring solar cycle forecasts by grounding forecast accuracy in operationally-relevant satellite lifetime predictions.
item.dc:creator: Scott Shambaugh

item.title: A Solar Optical Clock
item.description: arXiv:2610.28485v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Precision spectroscopy underpins quantum sensing, atomic timekeeping, and the search for terrestrial-mass exoplanets. Finding an Earth-Sun analog requires fractional splitting of spectral features that rivals the precision of the best laboratory spectroscopy. This corresponds to resolution of a few parts in $10^5$ of a typical stellar spectral line, or a Doppler velocity precision of less than 10 cm s$^{-1}$. Only a few astrophysical spectrometers reach this regime, and only by dispersing starlight with large gratings and averaging thousands of lines. Here, we show that comparable precision can be achieved on a single solar line by leveraging techniques used in quantum sensors and optical clocks. A laser is frequency-locked to the 1565 nm solar Fe I line by coupling to a single mode of the solar thermal field and counted against an optical frequency comb referenced to the SI second, thus creating a solar optical clock. Operating at the fundamental photon-noise limit of thermal heterodyne spectroscopy, we achieve centroid precision of one part in $10^9$ of the optical frequency, or 30 cm s$^{-1}$ in radial velocity. We recover the Sun's five-minute acoustic oscillations and the expected Rossiter-McLaughlin signal during a solar eclipse. Combining these techniques from quantum sensing with a thirty-meter-class telescope could enable our demonstrated precision on the nearest Sun-like stars in a few hours. Multiplexing such absolute frequency measurements across lines with different magnetic sensitivity and formation depth would reduce averaging time and help disentangle stellar granulation and activity from the Doppler signature of terrestrial exoplanets, providing new approaches to address some of the most demanding measurements in astrophysical spectroscopy.
item.dc:creator: Connor Fredrick, Ryan K. Cole, Ryan Terrien, Suvrath Mahadevan, Scott A. Diddams

item.title: Deep Learning Search for Gravitational Waves from Compact Binary Coalescence
item.description: arXiv:2603.09386v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gravitational-wave searches rely on a combination of methods, including matched filtering, coherent analyses, and more recent machine-learning-based pipelines. For compact binary coalescences --- where signals originate from the relativistic dynamics of compact objects --- matched filtering remains a central element, but its computational cost will increase substantially with the data volumes and parameter-space coverage required by next-generation interferometers such as the Einstein Telescope. Developing complementary strategies that reduce computational load while preserving detection performance is therefore essential. We investigate a hybrid approach that combines matched-filtering concepts with Convolutional Neural Networks, enabling efficient signal searches without relying on the usual $\chi^2$ rejection test. Using simulated data sets that include injected signals in Gaussian noise, transient noise, and physical effects not represented in the template bank --- such as eccentricity, precession and higher-order modes --- we show that the method achieves a detection efficiency comparable to or better than a standard matched-filtering search while offering a more resource-efficient pipeline in all the cases where the physics included in the signals were not represented in the template bank or when glitches were affecting the data. Conversely, the analysis also reveals some loss of detection capability for standard BNS/BBH searches in pure Gaussian noise. These results indicate that deep-learning-assisted searches can support sustainable gravitational-wave data analysis in future detector eras.
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Mobilia, Tito Dal Canton, Gianluca Maria Guidi

item.title: A Unified HI Rotation Curve Database for 122 Dwarf and Irregular Galaxies
item.description: arXiv:2605.22163v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a unified HI rotation curve database for 122 dwarf and irregular galaxies drawn from three Local Volume surveys, the Local Volume HI Survey (LVHIS; 32 galaxies), VLA-ANGST (29) and LITTLE THINGS (26), and from the WALLABY DR2 kinematic catalogue (35). The database provides standardised kinematic parameters, distance estimates, morphological classifications, and rotation curve data in machine-readable JSON, JSONL, and CSV formats with a documented schema, supporting retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications and cross-survey kinematic analysis. Quality tiers distinguish 26 galaxies with published tilted-ring rotation curves and per-point uncertainties from 96 automated-pipeline, single-ring or profile-width entries. Three worked examples demonstrate corpus queries, including evaluation of the $\omega$ estimator for DDO 154 (LITTLE THINGS). This work is presented as a data resource; no new dynamical model is proposed. This version describes corpus v1.3, which corrects the LITTLE THINGS curves (v1.1), the WALLABY entries (v1.2) and the LVHIS entries and reference (v1.3) of v1.0. The database and all computation scripts are available at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23503221).
item.dc:creator: David C. Flynn

item.title: The Stellar "Snake"-V: the census within 3 kpc in the Solar Neighborhood
item.description: arXiv:2607.00098v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a Gaia DR3 source-level catalogue of Stellar Snake complexes within 3 kpc of the Sun. We define a Stellar Snake as a mutually coherent association of stellar overdensities, characterised by consistent positions, kinematics, orbital invariants, and ages, rather than a single gravitationally bound object. Moving beyond catalogue searches seeded by known open clusters, our framework operates directly on Gaia sources to recover extended, low-density substructures and interconnecting stellar bridges. The multi-stage pipeline extracts statistically significant, non-overlapping base nodes, infers homogeneous parameters using a PointNet point-cloud regressor, and links these nodes into large-scale macro-structures in a nine-coordinate feature space spanning positions, velocities, age log t, and derived dynamical quantities (E, L_Z). After FoF-topology checking and boundary resolution, the final catalogue contains 1,180 Stellar Snake candidates with 4,196 base nodes and 692,408 unique member-star entries. Derived parameters are compared with external open-cluster catalogues and spectroscopic benchmarks. We introduce a graph-relation Snake Reliability Index (SRI) with Gold/Silver/Bronze grades to quantify structural coherence. A spatial-kinematic partition diagnostic identifies candidate subdivisions and provides core scores. At the population level, the catalogue shows an age--metallicity pattern in the jointly inferred parameters, a declining upper envelope of observed member-star entries toward older inferred ages, and a projected association between young Snake nodes, nearby spiral-arm loci, and the Radcliffe Wave. This homogeneous inventory provides an observational foundation for probing the formation, coherence, and dynamical evolution of hierarchical stellar complexes in the Milky Way.
item.dc:creator: Xiang-Ming Yang, Ju-Yong Zhang, Hai-Jun Tian

item.title: Impact of numerical stability in Bayesian noise wave calibration on global 21-cm experiments
item.description: arXiv:2607.26911v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Detecting the global 21-cm signal from the Cosmic Dawn and Epoch of Reionization requires calibration accuracy far below the level of astrophysical foregrounds. REACH models its receiver using the noise wave formalism, with five frequency-dependent low-noise amplifier parameters fitted jointly to multiple calibration sources. We identify a numerical instability in this Bayesian calibration pipeline: the condition number of the posterior covariance matrix reaches $\kappa(\mathbf{V}^*) \sim 10^{9}$--$10^{11}$, making solutions non-reproducible across computing environments. Singular value decomposition shows that the instability is driven by near-collinearity between the design-matrix columns associated with the excess noise source temperature, $X_\mathrm{NS}$, and the load temperature, $X_\mathrm{L}$. Using a Chebyshev basis, we develop a two-step mitigation. First, fixing $T_\mathrm{NS}$ to a scalar removes the degeneracy and reduces $\kappa(\mathbf{V}^*)$ to $\sim 60$. Second, to retain frequency dependence, we recover $T_\mathrm{NS}(\nu)$ directly from the hot-load calibration measurement. On mock data, this method preserves the stability of the reduced model while achieving comparable calibration accuracy. Masking narrow channels around cable standing-wave degeneracies further removes local artefacts in the design matrix. These steps provide a stable, reproducible, and data-driven calibration procedure. Because the $X_\mathrm{NS}$--$X_\mathrm{L}$ degeneracy is inherent to the noise wave formalism, the method is relevant to other global 21-cm experiments.
item.dc:creator: Saswata Dasgupta, Adarsh Kumar Dash, Dominic Anstey, Harry T. J. Bevins, Christian Kirkham, Eloy de Lera Acedo

item.title: Spectroscopic Binary Detection as Agent-Callable Tools: Detecting 40,000+ Main-Sequence Binary Candidates from SDSS DR19 APOGEE Spectra
item.description: arXiv:2608.10866v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unresolved binaries are common in spectroscopic surveys, and their blended light biases the parameters inferred for them. Methods to detect them exist, but applying one to a new data release is limited mostly by operating know-how that is rarely written down. We package the double-lined spectroscopic binary decomposition of El-Badry et al. (2018b) for reuse on APOGEE spectra, with the executable operations as nine tool servers built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the operating decisions as a Skill. Run over the 238,205 DR19 dwarfs under a fixed driver script, the classifier flags 41,466 SB2 candidates, about fifteen times the 2,645 identified in DR13, though not at matched purity. The 8.1% control false-positive rate implies that close to 40% are single stars, so we release the sample as a candidate list. The joint visit fit prefers two stars for 46% of the SB2 with multiple visits. Of these, 4,149 have velocity changes above 10 km/s. This cut is also passed by 7% of flagged single stars. The pipeline velocities identify another 3,943 velocity variables. We compare the eccentricities of the best-sampled binaries and find no significant difference between the close twins (q > 0.95) and matched non-twins, which excludes an eccentricity excess of the kind measured at wide separations. An ablation of two operating decisions illustrates that a fresh agent recovers a removed decision only when its absence leaves a measurable trace in the fit. We release the tools, the Skill, and the DR19 catalog with its multi-epoch supplement.
item.dc:creator: Serat M. Saad, Yuan-Sen Ting

item.title: Do Tabular Foundation Models Know Physics? Contamination, Units, and the Deterministic Limit
item.description: arXiv:2609.02766v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) learn to fill in tables the way language models fill in text --- and tables are arguably the format in which most physical measurement arrives. Did they learn any physics in the process? They are Bayesian by construction, so the question is what their prior contains. We probe it directly, evaluating four of them ($\texttt{TabPFN-3}$, $\texttt{TabICLv2}$, $\texttt{TabDPT}$ and $\texttt{Real-TabPFN-2.5}$) against six baselines on datasets sampled from 316 physical equations, in and out of domain. TFMs dominate, out of the box and after tuning. But they struggle to represent noiseless deterministic mechanisms in their uncertainty, and show no sign of exploiting physical units: they interpolate physics without yet being able to act as physical models.
item.dc:creator: Wassim Tenachi, Yashar Hezaveh, Laurence Perreault Levasseur, Pierre-Luc Bacon

item.title: Chana: A GPU-Accelerated Adaptive-Mesh Code for General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics with Multigroup M1 Neutrino Transport
item.description: arXiv:2610.07267v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper presents Chana, a GPU-accelerated, block-structured adaptive-mesh code for general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, multigroup M1 neutrino transport, and dynamical spacetime evolution using the Z4c formulation. Each physical module uses independently selected spatial discretizations and ghost-zone widths to balance accuracy and computational cost. Stiff radiation-matter interactions are treated implicitly, with Jacobians calculated analytically from the chain-rules. The code is written in C++20 and it uses MPI and Kokkos 5 for distributed-memory and performance-portable parallelism. The code is validated through a number of GRMHD, radiation transport, and dynamic spacetime tests. For a representative core-collapse supernova configuration with three neutrino species and 12 energy groups per species, the code achieves approximately $1.1 \times 10^6$ cell updates per GPU second on NVIDIA A100 GPUs using four-stage RK4 integration. Weak-scaling efficiency remains above 85\% up to 256 GPUs on Perlmutter.
item.dc:creator: Tianshu Wang
